evidence:
Gopal has his father's sale deed from 1989, the 1996 survey map, tax receipts in the family's name since 1990, and his own inheritance record from 2012. He has dated photographs of the plot from 2015 showing the coconut trees and irrigation channel, but the photos do not clearly show a boundary line. A hand-drawn sketch by a retired village officer, signed but undated, supports Gopal's approximate dimensions.

Mahesh has his deed from 2017 and a statement from an elderly farmer who says the "old boundary" ran along the channel as long as he remembers. The channel has been re-dug at least once, so its current position may not match the original. No fresh professional survey exists, and satellite images show the coconut trees in a line but cannot establish legal boundaries. Fence construction photos from last month show Gopal standing nearby without objecting at the time, which Mahesh may use as acquiescence.

events.description: plot from his father in 2012 and has farmed vegetables on it since.
His neighbor, Mahesh Patil, bought the adjoining plot in 2017.
Last month, Mahesh built a permanent brick fence that Gopal says cuts about 3 meters into his land along a 40-meter stretch, taking roughly 120 sq.
Mahesh says the fence follows the "old boundary" that has been in place for decades, marked by a row of coconut trees and an irrigation channel, and that Gopal's father never objected.

Gopal's sale deed describes boundaries by reference to neighbors and landmarks rather than exact measurements, and a government survey map from 1996 shows the plot as a rough polygon with different dimensions from those in the deed.
Mahesh's deed uses different landmarks, and one of them, a "village footpath," no longer exists.
Mahesh has told Gopal that if he wants the fence moved, he must go to court, and that he will claim the land by long possession if needed.
Gopal wants the fence removed, wants to know which documents will carry the most weight, and fears that years of acquiescence by his father may now count against him.

evidence_plan.heading: Evidence plan
prompts: Which part of the timeline needs independent support?
What already shows that event, and who may lawfully hold another record?

suggestions.title: Possession, title and notices
suggestions.look_for: Gather records you already hold, such as agreements, deeds, orders, rent payments or notices. Note who occupied the property and when that changed.
suggestions.why: Documents and the timeline can help distinguish possession from a claim about legal ownership.
suggestions.action: Keep full copies and record where each came from. Request records through the issuing office or a lawyer when needed.

suggestions.title: Location and visible changes
suggestions.look_for: Note the address or boundary reference and any changed lock, barrier or damage you actually observed.
suggestions.why: This helps identify the location and the particular change in dispute.
suggestions.action: Document only from an area you may safely and lawfully access. Do not enter disputed space or confront anyone.

suggestions.title: Purchase, promised terms and communications
suggestions.look_for: Look for the order confirmation, invoice, payment record and relevant warranty or service terms. Keep the complete email or chat thread.
suggestions.why: These can show what was purchased, what was promised and what resolution the seller offered.
suggestions.action: Keep the original files or exports. Record dates and ask for copies from the seller or platform if you do not have them.

suggestions.title: Condition of the product or work
suggestions.look_for: If safe, note the model or order number, the fault and when it appeared. Keep existing dated photos, service requests or repair reports.
suggestions.why: A dated record helps distinguish what you observed from a possible explanation of the fault.
suggestions.action: Leave suspected electrical or other hazardous damage to a qualified person. Ask the repair provider for a written report if they inspect it.

suggestions.title: Original records and an evidence log
suggestions.look_for: Keep records you lawfully have, with their surrounding context. For each item note the related event, who provided it, when you received it, and any transfer.
suggestions.why: The log distinguishes what you observed from what someone later told you and makes it easier to check the source.
suggestions.action: Keep an unchanged original and label working copies. Avoid editing originals, guessing gaps, or sharing evidence publicly.

suggestions.title: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy
suggestions.reference: Civil Appeal 6191 of 2001 · para. 17, PDF pp. 6–7
suggestions.takeaway: The Court distinguished interference with possession from disputes where title or recovery of possession also needs to be decided.
suggestions.difference: Compare who possessed the property, whether title is seriously disputed, and the relief sought. The decision concerned competing claims to vacant plots.
suggestions.connection: Your account raises an issue about possession, ownership or interference with land.
suggestions.preparation: Work out who currently has possession, whether ownership is disputed and what order you want the court to make.
